core composition. A critique may identify a missing AXI ordering assumption. A
learned method, script, or engineer may return a repaired artifact. Interface
and implementation tools check stated properties. A harness coordinates
compatible RTL, compiler, workload, and tool state. An analysis method or
architect explains whether data movement, computation, or another mechanism
changed the system result. These roles produce the different outputs in
@tbl-method-role-handoffs, but critique, repair, checking, explanation, and
coordination are not additional method families. None of them must be
performed by a learned component.

Component boundaries should follow method fit rather than the number of roles.
One component may perform several roles when its inputs, outputs, allowed
actions, cost, stopping conditions, and required checks remain clear. Split
the work when those requirements differ or when a shared component would judge
assumptions it created itself. A split adds a handoff and does not by itself
make the judgment independent. Any claim of independence must be supported by
a sufficiently different execution, checking, or review path together with
the shared assumptions that remain. The resulting combinations differ in when
they are justified and in what keeps them minimal
(@tbl-method-organization).

| **Composition** | **When it is justified** | **What keeps it minimal** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conventional technique or direct tools | Existing calculations, builders, solvers, heuristics, or evaluations can perform the job economically. | Add no learned component unless it removes distinct work without weakening the check. |
| Generation only | Useful artifacts are missing and direct checking is affordable. | Stop when enough useful candidates exist or review becomes limiting. |
| Prediction only | Existing candidates need cheap screening before costly evaluation. | Retain the predictor only while calibration and confirmation cost less than direct evaluation. |
| Optimization only | A conventional objective can guide selection over a space too large to enumerate. | Compare with a strong simple baseline and stop when further selection cannot change the decision economically. |
| Generation plus prediction | Candidate construction is needed, but most proposals cannot afford direct evaluation. | The predictor screens only the consequence for which compatible support exists. |
| Generation plus optimization | Candidate construction is needed, and the evaluation budget requires selective search, but no supported surrogate is available. | The optimizer uses direct feedback and each generated candidate still passes the declared checks. |
| Prediction plus optimization | A surrogate makes selective search economical under expensive feedback. | Keep the surrogate, acquisition rule, and later confirmation separately inspectable. |
| Generation, prediction, and optimization | Missing artifacts, costly evaluation, and selective search all limit the same study. | Each component has a distinct input, output, action, cost, and stopping condition. |

: **A component earns its place by performing necessary work that another
component does not.** Adding more models or agents is not itself a stronger
method. {#tbl-method-organization tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

Read the first four rows as single-family or direct choices, the next three as
two-family compositions, and the final row as the case in which all three jobs
are independently necessary. The last column supplies the limiting condition
for each composition. The table does not recommend adding components in that
order. Each row applies only when its named work is missing and its stopping
condition keeps the added component economical.

## Worked Method Decisions

The same decision fields expose why two familiar systems need different
compositions (@tbl-worked-method-decisions). KernelBench evaluates
language-model generation of graphics processing unit (GPU) kernels with a
fixed compiler, correctness harness, and performance baseline
[@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench]. AutoTVM and Ansor tune tensor programs by
combining candidate construction, learned cost prediction, search,
compilation, and target measurement
[@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor].

### Constrained Generation and Compiler Tuning

| **Decision field** | **Constrained kernel generation** | **Compiler tuning** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Role | Construct a target-specific kernel that preserves the operator's semantics and may improve measured performance. | Construct or select a schedule that improves a declared operator on a named target. |
| Family | Generation. Conventional compilation, correctness checking, and measurement are part of the composed evaluation path. | Generation, prediction, and optimization. Conventional compilation and target measurement are part of the composed evaluation path. |
| Technique | An LLM produces kernel code under fixed semantics, shapes, data types, and target constraints. | AutoTVM uses schedule templates, a learned cost model, and simulated-annealing search; Ansor uses program construction, a learned cost model, and evolutionary search. |
| Inputs | Operator definition, tensor shapes, data types, numerical tolerance, target GPU, permitted transformations, and starting context. | Operator or workload, target hardware, legal schedule or program space, compiler state, prior observations, and evaluation budget. |
| Evaluator | A fixed compiler and external correctness harness reject unusable kernels before target timing compares accepted artifacts. | The compiler and target measurements evaluate selected schedules under common semantics and conditions. |
| Feedback cost | Failed generations, compilation, correctness runs, target executions, model use, and expert review. | Cost-model fitting, candidate construction, search, compilation, target runs, and tuning review. |
| Fallback | Stop learned generation when it cannot produce a checked artifact within budget and use the predeclared conventional constructor. | Fall back to the compiler default, an optimized library, an expert schedule, or a conventional autotuner fixed before comparison. |
| Strong practical conventional alternative | A predeclared optimized library, compiler-fusion path, parameterized template, or conventional autotuner under the same checks and budget. | The strongest available library or compiler schedule, expert heuristic, or conventional autotuner under matched target measurements and total cost. |

: **The missing capability determines the composition.** Kernel construction
needs generation only when the artifact is absent, while compiler tuning may
need construction, prediction, and selective search because target measurements
are costly. Both retain a conventional fallback and the same external
evaluator.
{#tbl-worked-method-decisions tbl-colwidths="[18,41,41]"}

Read each column from the role to the fallback. The generation case succeeds
only when the fixed compiler and correctness harness accept the artifact; a
checker generated from the same prompt would not automatically supply an
independent oracle. The compiler-tuning case separates the learned cost model
from the search procedure and from target measurement. AutoTVM and Ansor
combine those parts differently, which is evidence against treating one
component order as universal.

The strongest practical conventional alternative must be selected for the
actual operator and target rather than inferred from a generic method label.
The current KernelBench evidence does not establish which library, compiler,
template, or conventional autotuner is strongest for every generated task.
That unresolved choice belongs in the comparison setup, not in a post-result
explanation.

### Direct Evaluation for the Lighthouse Study

The represented cache study needs an approach decision before
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces builds the execution
environment. The smallest justified approach is direct tool evaluation. The
declared SRAM limits control whether a candidate is dispatched to cycle-level
simulation, with no added generator, predictor, or optimizer.
The complete request connects that decision to its inputs, actions, budget,
tools, and later checks (@tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision).

| **Decision field** | **`XR-L2-CAP-A` approach** |
| --- | --- |
| Job | Compare the represented 2\ MB baseline with the 3\ MB and 4\ MB alternatives without widening the study. |
| Selected approach | Evaluate the existing represented artifacts. Run one `SRAM-A` evaluation per capacity, then use a shared rerun of the 2\ MB baseline and matched `SIM-A` executions for the candidates that satisfy the declared SRAM limits. No added generator, predictor, or optimizer is used. |
| Why this fits | The candidate set is complete and contains only three values. The live history is empty. Direct evaluation is affordable within the declared budget. |
| Inputs | `XR-L2-CAP-A`, `CONTRACT-A`, `XR-COMPUTE-A`, the fixed hardware and software identifiers, `XR-TRACE-A`, the three candidate artifacts, and the declared limits and exclusions from @sec-data-representations-world-models. |
| Output | A bounded tool request for each `SRAM-A` area, access-time, and cache-local energy and leakage result; the shared rerun baseline; matched frame data and 99th-percentile frame time from `SIM-A`; capacity misses from `CACHE-A`; and subsystem dynamic and leakage power from `PM-A`. This chapter does not interpret the returned results. |
| Allowed actions | Select only `l2.capacity` values `2MB`, `3MB`, or `4MB`; request declared evaluations; change no cache policy, associativity, NoC, compiler, runtime, workload, or other architecture field. |
| Planned cost | Three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, plus configuration checks and review. |
| Stopping conditions | Stop when the decision is resolved, all eligible capacities are evaluated, the cycle-level budget is spent, a required input or tool is unavailable, or no alternative passes the SRAM limits. |
| Requested tools | `SRAM-A` under `PVT-A` for modeled area, access time, and cache-local energy and leakage, followed by `SIM-A` with `CACHE-A` and `PM-A` under the fixed workload and software conditions. `PM-A` returns subsystem dynamic plus leakage power rather than substituting the cache-local result. The environment must retain matched frame identifiers, tool and model identities, failures, and budget consumption. |
| Required later checks | Confirm candidate and condition identity. Check modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power at or below 3\ W, macro area at or below 1.5\ mm^2^, and modeled access time at or below 2.5\ ns. Estimate frame-time reduction with a 95 percent interval over matched contiguous baseline and candidate frame groups; @sec-feedback-verification-trust owns the statistical procedure and qualification. At most one candidate may advance, and only if its physical checks pass and the interval relative to the 2\ MB rerun baseline lies above zero. Retain cache misses by classification, including capacity misses, for the later mechanism check. Thermal and IR-drop reviews remain independent later requirements. |

: **The Lighthouse study chooses direct evaluation.** The represented problem
is small enough that the declared SRAM dispatch check and cycle-level
comparison cost less than adding generation, predictor calibration, or search
setup.
{#tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision tbl-colwidths="[21,69]"}

Read downward from the job, selected approach, and reason for choosing it to
the inputs, outputs, and actions that keep the study bounded. The final rows
turn that choice into an executable budget, stopping conditions, tool requests,
and later checks. The critical separation is between the SRAM dispatch check
and the later cycle-level comparison. The first can decide which candidates
spend scarce executions, but it cannot interpret the returned architecture
result.

The serious current alternative sends all three capacities through `SIM-A`
without waiting for the SRAM screen. It uses the same represented state, action
space, tools, and total cycle-level budget. It is not selected because the
cheap physical screen can reject a capacity before that capacity spends a
scarce cycle-level execution.

A calibrated predictor with sequential experiment selection is a future
revisit condition, not an alternative in the current study definition. It becomes
reasonable only if the legal cache space expands, direct evaluation becomes
the limiting cost, and compatible observations are added to the represented
problem.

The study rejects an unnecessary method, not AI-assisted architecture as a
whole.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces now receives a concrete request
for real tools rather than a generic instruction to build an AI environment.

## Open Research Questions

The open problems concern method fit before deployment, support after a design
problem changes, and composition when feedback is costly.

### Predicting Method Fit

**How can an architect estimate total method cost before committing to an
added method?** Setup, calibration, execution, checking, and review are visible
at different times, which makes the comparison hardest when it matters most.

**How can a study predict which technique will outperform the strongest
practical conventional alternative?** Question type, data support, search
structure, evaluator quality, and failure consequence interact, so a family
label alone cannot answer the question.

### Preserving Legality and Support

**How can generation preserve legality without eliminating the alternatives
that matter?** Grammar and schema constraints can enforce selected properties,
but physical feasibility and useful diversity remain harder to balance.

**How should a predictor declare and test its support for a changing
architecture study?** Workloads, design regions, tools, and process assumptions
move together, so a useful support statement must be more specific than a
single uncertainty score. An architecture world model adds the further
question of which state transitions remain supported after the action space or
tool path changes.

### Composing Under Costly Feedback

**How much of a selected candidate's predicted gain survives stronger
evaluation?** Optimizer's curse depends on candidate-pool size, prediction
error, and selection policy, and architecture studies need practical ways to
anticipate that shrinkage.

**How should a composition adapt when its limiting capability changes?**
Prediction, generation, optimization, and direct tools can precede or follow
one another. The open problem is to change the composition without losing the
external check, matched cost accounting, or a viable fallback.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Choose the smallest method that preserves the check"}
Name the role before choosing a family, choose the technique only after
examining its fit, and add components only when each performs necessary work.
Fit includes the question type, data support, search structure, evaluator,
total feedback cost, runtime and locality limits, reliability, reversibility,
and failure consequence. State the external check that can reject the output;
a generated checker is not automatically independent.
:::

Prediction is useful when direct evaluation is too costly and compatible
observations can support an estimate. An architecture world model is one
transition-aware predictive technique, not a universal model of architecture.
Generation is useful when a required artifact or alternative is missing and an
external tool path can reject an invalid result. Optimization is useful when a
legal search space exceeds the evaluation budget; multiobjective optimization
can expose a Pareto frontier, but it cannot decide the architect's tradeoff.
Conventional techniques often provide the strongest practical implementation,
baseline, or fallback for these families.

These families do not impose a fixed order. Start with the missing capability,
then move among construction, estimation, selection, and direct evaluation as
feedback changes the work. Kernel generation requires an external compiler and
correctness harness, while compiler tuning may combine construction, a learned
cost model, search, compilation, and target measurement. The components and
their order are justified by the problem, not copied from a generic stack.

The Lighthouse study makes that principle concrete. Three declared capacities,
no compatible live history, and four cycle-level executions do not justify a
learned stack. Deterministic SRAM screening and direct matched comparison are
the stronger choice. It demonstrates that using no added predictor, generator,
or optimizer can be the deliberate smallest-sufficient decision.

@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces receives the resulting bounded
tool request. It must construct the environment that can execute `SRAM-A` and
`SIM-A` against the represented candidate and condition identities, return
inspectable results, and stop within the declared budget.
